newsitem.title: GERMANY: SOCCER SHOWCASE-CONTRASTING PRIORITIES FOR TWO BORUSSIAS.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER SHOWCASE-CONTRASTING PRIORITIES FOR TWO BORUSSIAS.

text.p: They carry the same name from history but Borussia Moenchengladbach and Borussia Dortmund have contrasting predicaments and priorities as they prepare for Saturday's German league match in Dortmund.
The name "Borussia" is a derivation of Prussia, the former powerful eastern German state of the 19th century.

While many football experts are unsure exactly how Borussia got into the name of the two clubs, it is likely to have come from the Prussians who moved west to find work in the industrial areas around Dortmund and Moenchengladbach.
Both western German clubs were set up at the start of this century. They have experienced contrasting times since German league football began with the Bundesliga in 1963.

Moenchengladbach enjoyed their heyday in the 1970s when the likes of Guenter Netzer, present national team coach Berti Vogts, Jupp Heynckes and Rainer Bonhof guided the club to five league championships.

Some of their legendary battles with Bayern Munich for the title are still shown on television. The two clubs' players made up much of the German team which won the World Cup in 1974 under Franz Beckenbauer.

Moenchengladbach also won the UEFA Cup in 1975 and 1979. They were a household name across Europe even though most football fans outside of Germany struggled to pronounce their name properly. Spelling it was out of the question.
Dortmund have a very different history. Although they were German pioneers in Europe with their European Cup Winners' Cup triumph in 1966, their best years, by contrast, have come in the 1990s.
Playing virtually every game in front of a full house, their success is built on shrewd marketing and a handful of internationals who have carried the club to the title in the last two seasons.
Dortmund, along with Bayern, have replaced Moenchengladbach as the main source of international players. Germany won last year's European championship in England.
The two clubs face different problems as the season moves towards its decisive stage with Saturday's game in Dortmund.
Despite a 4-1 defeat at VfB Stuttgart last weekend, European Cup campaigners Dortmund are still on top of the table and looking forward to more lucrative income from European football next season.
After finishing fourth last season and winning the German Cup in 1995, Moenchengladbach suffered a disastrous first half of the season and are struggling near the bottom of the table.
The return to form of their key midfielder Stefan Effenberg is vital to their chances of avoiding the drop. A return to European football and its lucrative television revenue is out of the question.
